text: This is Make Good: product recall refunds through PayPal, with proof behind every payment.

When a supplier recalls one faulty batch, a small shop faces a hard question. Which customers actually received that batch? PayPal knows who paid, but not which batch anyone got. And the shop's own records disagree: product codes typed differently, missing batch numbers, two payments under one order number. So the shop either refunds everyone and loses money, or it waits, and customers open disputes and chargebacks. Either way, trust breaks.

Make Good answers two separate questions for every buyer. Is this really their PayPal payment? And was their unit affected? Proven cases go onto one exact payment list that a person approves. Unclear cases are held, and the customer can simply be asked. Then PayPal refunds each customer once, confirmed by PayPal itself, and each one is told. People are made whole before anyone needs to open a dispute.

It's built with Node and TypeScript on Fastify, with PostgreSQL. Money moves through the PayPal REST APIs for refunds, payouts and dispute checks, tested on the real PayPal sandbox. Google Gemini can read the supplier's notice, and Playwright tests the whole page in a real browser.

caption: Open the recall case
text: Let's walk through it. Press Open the recall case. It loads thirty-two invented orders on a built-in PayPal simulator, and the labels on the left say so on every screen.

caption: The sidebar: done, do this now, next step
text: The sidebar is your map. Ticks show what's done, Do this now marks the current step, and the blue Next step button always takes you there.

caption: Step 1 · Read the supplier's notice
text: Step one reads the supplier's notice. Here the built-in rules read it; with a Gemini key, Gemini does. Every line quotes the notice word for word, and nothing applies until a person saves the rules.

caption: Step 2 · Two questions for every buyer
text: Step two finds the affected customers. Each buyer gets two answers, crossed in this table. Green is ready to refund, amber needs a person. Look-alike codes, like HM-3000, are decided by a person, never guessed.

caption: Step 3 · The Recovery Map and the evidence
text: Step three is the Recovery Map: every buyer, and why they stand where they do. Open a customer to see the facts. This order shipped while two batches were going out, so it's held, not paid.

caption: Ask the customer with a one-time link
text: When the records can't settle it, email the customer a one-time link. They type the batch code from the box. Their answer becomes evidence, and staff still decide.

caption: Step 4 · Three refund policies, priced
text: Step four prices three refund policies on these records: what each would cost, and who a looser rule would pay by mistake.

caption: Step 5 · Approve one exact payment list
text: Step five builds one exact payment list, with a version and a fingerprint. If anything changes after approval, the approval is withdrawn.

caption: Step 6 · Pay through PayPal, even when a reply is lost
text: Step six pays through PayPal. To test it, we make PayPal lose one reply. That payment shows as unknown, not failed. Make Good asks PayPal again with the same request ID and gets the same refund back. Nobody is paid twice.

caption: Customers told, results checked, every step audited
text: Customers are emailed only after PayPal confirms. The results are checked against the known answers of this test data, and every action sits on an audit trail that can't be edited.

Why trust it? Every screen labels what's simulated. The same case ran on the real PayPal sandbox, with sixteen real refunds and PayPal's own IDs on record. A hundred and twenty automated tests and a browser test run with one command. And you can test it your way: upload your own orders, send yourself the customer link, or make PayPal lose a reply.
Make Good. The right customers, refunded once, with proof.
